claim: A method has been developed to introduce novel paratopes into the human antibody repertoire by modifying the immunoglobulin (Ig) genes of mature B cells directly using genome editing technologies.
source: We have developed a method to introduce novel paratopes into the human antibody repertoire by modifying the immunoglobulin (Ig) genes of mature B cells directly using genome editing technologies.
evidence: The abstract directly states the development of this method as a primary finding of the study.

claim: CRISPR-Cas9 was used in a homology directed repair strategy to replace the heavy chain (HC) variable region in B cell lines with that from HIV broadly neutralizing antibody PG9.
source: We used CRISPR-Cas9 in a homology directed repair strategy, to replace the heavy chain (HC) variable region in B cell lines with that from an HIV broadly neutralizing antibody (bnAb), PG9.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes the use of CRISPR-Cas9 and the specific antibody used.

claim: The engineering strategy is designed to function in cells that have undergone VDJ recombination using any combination of variable (V), diversity (D) and joining (J) genes.
source: Our strategy is designed to function in cells that have undergone VDJ recombination using any combination of variable (V), diversity (D) and joining (J) genes.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the design goal of universal applicability across VDJ recombination events.

claim: The modified locus expresses PG9 HC which pairs with native light chains (LCs) resulting in the cell surface expression of HIV specific B cell receptors (BCRs).
source: The modified locus expresses PG9 HC which pairs with native light chains (LCs) resulting in the cell surface expression of HIV specific B cell receptors (BCRs).
evidence: The abstract directly states this outcome of the engineering strategy.

claim: Endogenous activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) in engineered cells allowed for Ig class switching.
source: Endogenous activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) in engineered cells allowed for Ig class switching and generated BCR variants with improved HIV neutralizing activity.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that AID enabled class switching in engineered cells.

claim: Endogenous AID in engineered cells generated BCR variants with improved HIV neutralizing activity.
source: Endogenous activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) in engineered cells allowed for Ig class switching and generated BCR variants with improved HIV neutralizing activity.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that AID activity led to improved neutralizing variants.

claim: BCRs engineered in this way retain the genetic flexibility normally required for affinity maturation during adaptive immune responses.
source: Thus, BCRs engineered in this way retain the genetic flexibility normally required for affinity maturation during adaptive immune responses.
evidence: The abstract explicitly concludes that engineered BCRs maintain genetic flexibility for affinity maturation.

claim: Peripheral blood derived primary B cells from three different donors were edited using this strategy.
source: Peripheral blood derived primary B cells from three different donors were edited using this strategy.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the number of donors and cell type used.

claim: Engineered primary B cells could bind the PG9 epitope.
source: Engineered cells could bind the PG9 epitope and sequenced mRNA showed PG9 HC transcribed as several different isotypes after culture with CD40 ligand and IL-4.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that engineered cells bound the PG9 epitope.

claim: Sequenced mRNA showed PG9 HC transcribed as several different isotypes after culture with CD40 ligand and IL-4.
source: Engineered cells could bind the PG9 epitope and sequenced mRNA showed PG9 HC transcribed as several different isotypes after culture with CD40 ligand and IL-4.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes the mRNA sequencing results showing multiple isotypes.

claim: Protective antibodies against some pathogens require features not easily elicited through affinity maturation from the human antibody repertoire.
source: Protective antibodies against some pathogens require features not easily elicited through affinity maturation from the human antibody repertoire (Kepler and Wiehe, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kepler and Wiehe, 2017.

claim: Antibodies with protective paratopes encoded mostly within their HCs exist.
source: The existence of antibodies with protective paratopes encoded mostly within their HCs (Heydarchi et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2017; Sok et al., 2017; Sui et al., 2009) suggested that it might be possible to achieve this goal through replacement of the recombined HC variable region alone.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Heydarchi et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2017; Sok et al., 2017; Sui et al., 2009).

claim: Broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) against HIV are protective.
source: We used HIV as a model because, while broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) against this virus are protective (Pegu et al., 2017) and their gene sequences have been well defined (McCoy and Burton, 2017), they remain exceedingly difficult to elicit by vaccination (Mascola and Haynes, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pegu et al., 2017.

claim: HIV bnAb gene sequences have been well defined.
source: We used HIV as a model because, while broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) against this virus are protective (Pegu et al., 2017) and their gene sequences have been well defined (McCoy and Burton, 2017), they remain exceedingly difficult to elicit by vaccination (Mascola and Haynes, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to McCoy and Burton, 2017.

claim: HIV bnAbs remain exceedingly difficult to elicit by vaccination.
source: We used HIV as a model because, while broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) against this virus are protective (Pegu et al., 2017) and their gene sequences have been well defined (McCoy and Burton, 2017), they remain exceedingly difficult to elicit by vaccination (Mascola and Haynes, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mascola and Haynes, 2013.

claim: The breadth and neutralization potency of a number of bnAbs targeting the HIV Envelope glycoprotein (Env) 'V2 apex' region are largely encoded within unusually long HC complementarity-determining region 3 (CDRH3) loops.
source: Previous studies have suggested that the breadth and neutralization potency of a number of bnAbs targeting the HIV Envelope glycoprotein (Env) 'V2 apex' region are largely encoded within unusually long HC complementarity-determining region 3 (CDRH3) loops, which form the majority of contacts with Env (Julien et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2017; McLellan et al., 2011; Pejchal et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Julien et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2017; McLellan et al., 2011; Pejchal et al., 2010).

claim: The CDRH3 loops of V2 apex-targeting bnAbs form the majority of contacts with Env.
source: Previous studies have suggested that the breadth and neutralization potency of a number of bnAbs targeting the HIV Envelope glycoprotein (Env) 'V2 apex' region are largely encoded within unusually long HC complementarity-determining region 3 (CDRH3) loops, which form the majority of contacts with Env (Julien et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2017; McLellan et al., 2011; Pejchal et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Julien et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2017; McLellan et al., 2011; Pejchal et al., 2010).

claim: The IgG HC from the V2 apex-targeting bnAb PG9 could pair and be secreted with a diversity of lambda (λ) and kappa (k) LCs when co-transfected in HEK293 cells.
source: We found that the IgG HC from the V2 apex-targeting bnAb PG9 could pair and be secreted with a diversity of lambda (λ) and kappa (k) LCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) when co-transfected in HEK293 cells.
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing the diversity of LCs tested.

claim: SEC profiles and SDS-PAGE gels of secreted PG9 chimeric antibodies were comparable with the normal PG9 HC/LC pair.
source: Size exclusion chromatography (SEC) profiles and SDS-PAGE gels of these secreted chimeric antibodies were comparable with the normal PG9 HC/LC pair (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The text states this comparison and references Figure 1—figure supplement 2 showing the SEC and SDS-PAGE data.

claim: All PG9 chimeric antibodies neutralized one or more of the PG9-sensitive viruses.
source: All PG9 chimeric antibodies neutralized one or more of the PG9-sensitive viruses, and most neutralized multiple viruses from different clades in the global panel (Figure 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 1 showing neutralization data.

claim: Most PG9 chimeric antibodies neutralized multiple viruses from different clades in the global panel.
source: All PG9 chimeric antibodies neutralized one or more of the PG9-sensitive viruses, and most neutralized multiple viruses from different clades in the global panel (Figure 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 1 showing neutralization data.

claim: No chimeric antibody was as broadly neutralizing as the original PG9 HC/LC pair.
source: No chimeric antibody was as broadly neutralizing as the original PG9 HC/LC pair, indicating significant LC-dependent restriction to neutralization breadth for this HIV bnAb.
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from the neutralization assays.

claim: There is significant LC-dependent restriction to neutralization breadth for the HIV bnAb PG9.
source: No chimeric antibody was as broadly neutralizing as the original PG9 HC/LC pair, indicating significant LC-dependent restriction to neutralization breadth for this HIV bnAb.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that no chimera matched the original PG9 breadth.

claim: Most PG9 chimeras had measurable binding affinity to 5 strains of recombinant soluble HIV envelope native trimers (SOSIPs) by biolayer interferometry (BLI).
source: Most chimeras had measurable binding affinity to 5 strains of recombinant soluble HIV envelope native trimers (SOSIPs) (Andrabi et al., 2015; Voss et al., 2017) by biolayer interferometry (BLI) (Frenzel and Willbold, 2014) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 1—figure supplement 3 showing BLI data.

claim: Autoreactivity was detected for about 60% of PG9 chimeras in the HEp-2 assay.
source: Autoreactivity was detected for about 60% of PG9 chimeras in the HEp-2 assay (Copple et al., 2012) as might be expected because of novel HC/LC interfaces in these antibodies (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 1—figure supplement 4 showing HEp-2 assay results.

claim: The autoreactivity of PG9 chimeras might be expected because of novel HC/LC interfaces in these antibodies.
source: Autoreactivity was detected for about 60% of PG9 chimeras in the HEp-2 assay (Copple et al., 2012) as might be expected because of novel HC/LC interfaces in these antibodies (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural changes introduced by chimeric pairing.

claim: It is possible to replace segments of genomic DNA in eukaryotic cells by introducing double strand DNA (dsDNA) breaks on either side of the segment in the presence of exogenous donor DNA that will be incorporated between these break sites by host cell DNA repair machinery.
source: It is possible to replace segments of genomic DNA in eukaryotic cells by introducing double strand DNA (dsDNA) breaks on either side of the segment in the presence of exogenous donor DNA that will be incorporated between these break sites by host cell DNA repair machinery.
evidence: This is established knowledge about genome editing mechanisms.

claim: Replacement DNA must be flanked by regions of sequence homology (HR) to the genome upstream and downstream of the two break sites in order to be incorporated by homology directed repair (HDR) mechanisms.
source: This replacement DNA must be flanked by regions of sequence homology (HR) to the genome upstream and downstream of the two break sites in order to be incorporated by homology directed repair (HDR) mechanisms (Doudna and Charpentier, 2014; Schwank et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about HDR mechanisms, supported by citations (Doudna and Charpentier, 2014; Schwank et al., 2013).

claim: Each human B cell undergoes genomic rearrangements during its genesis to assemble the HC VDJ gene from 1 of at least 55 functional V genes, 1 of 23 functional D genes, and 1 of 6 functional J genes.
source: This is because each human B cell undergoes genomic rearrangements during its genesis to assemble the HC VDJ gene from; 1 of at least 55 functional V genes (along with its individual 5' promoter); 1 of 23 functional D genes; and 1 of 6 functional J genes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about B cell development and VDJ recombination.

claim: The VDJ gene segments span nearly one megabase (Mb) when in germline configuration and constitute the immunoglobulin heavy chain variable (IGHV) locus on chromosome 14 (at 14q32.33).
source: Together, these gene segments span nearly one megabase (Mb) when in germline configuration and constitute the immunoglobulin heavy chain variable (IGHV) locus on chromosome 14 (at 14q32.33) (Giudicelli et al., 2005; Watson and Breden, 2012) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the IGHV locus, supported by citations (Giudicelli et al., 2005; Watson and Breden, 2012) and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A long-range HDR strategy was developed that introduced dsDNA breaks after the most 5' V-gene promoter (V7-81), and after the most distal J gene (J6), because HRs 5' and 3' to these sites respectively are retained in all B cells.
source: To respond to this challenge, we developed a long-range HDR strategy that introduced dsDNA breaks after the most 5' V-gene promoter (V7-81), and after the most distal J gene (J6), because HRs 5' and 3' to these sites respectively are retained in all B cells.
evidence: The text explicitly describes the development of this strategy and the rationale.

claim: The distance between the V7-81 and J6 cut sites will vary depending on which V and J genes were assembled in a given B cell.
source: The distance between these cut sites will vary depending on which V and J genes were assembled in a given B cell.
evidence: This is an inference based on the variable nature of VDJ recombination.

claim: The editing strategy introduces the new VDJ gene in a way that allows transcription using a naturally regulated V-gene promoter from its native locus where it would be subject to hypermutation by AID.
source: Thus, regardless of which genes were previously assembled, our editing strategy introduces the new VDJ gene in a way that allows transcription using a naturally regulated V-gene promoter from its native locus where it would be subject to hypermutation by AID.
evidence: The text explicitly describes this design feature of the editing strategy.

claim: When paired with an endogenous cell LC, a chimeric immunoglobulin (Ig) will be secreted as the isotype determined by the genomic configuration of the HC constant region in the engineered cell.
source: When paired with an endogenous cell LC, a chimeric immunoglobulin (Ig) will be secreted as the isotype determined by the genomic configuration of the HC constant region in the engineered cell.
evidence: This is an inference based on the design of the editing strategy.

claim: The Ramos (RA 1) B cell lymphoma line expresses an Ig HC that uses the IGHV4-34 (V), IGHD3-10 (D) and IGHJ6 (J) genes as IgM.
source: This human monoclonal line expresses an Ig HC that uses the IGHV4-34 (V), IGHD3-10 (D) and IGHJ6 (J) genes as IgM (Borchert et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Ramos cell line, supported by citation (Borchert et al., 2010).

claim: V4-34 lies halfway through the IGHV locus placing the 5' most V-gene promoter (V7-81) about 0.5 Mb upstream.
source: V4-34 lies halfway through the IGHV locus placing the 5' most V-gene promoter (V7-81) about 0.5 Mb upstream (Figure 2A).
evidence: The text states this genomic relationship and references Figure 2A showing the locus structure.

claim: A Ramos-specific engineering strategy was developed that introduced a dsDNA cut 3' of the V4-34 promoter and used donor DNA with a V4-34 promoter sequence 5' HR.
source: In addition to our universal B cell editing strategy, which grafts the PG9 VDJ gene between the V7-81 promoter and J6 splice site (Figure 2B), we developed an engineering strategy specific for this line that introduced a dsDNA cut 3' of the V4-34 promoter (instead of the V7-81), and which used donor DNA with a V4-34 promoter sequence 5' HR (Figure 2C).
evidence: The text explicitly describes this strategy and references Figure 2C showing the design.

claim: The Ramos-specific strategy replaces only the 400 bp Ramos VDJ rather than a 0.5 Mb region using the 'universal' BCR editing strategy.
source: This strategy replaces only the 400 bp Ramos VDJ rather than a 0.5 Mb region using the 'universal' BCR editing strategy.
evidence: The text explicitly states the difference in the size of DNA replaced between the two strategies.

claim: Cells engineered by the V434 or V781 strategies reproducibly converted an average of 1.75%(SD = 0.20) or 0.21%(SD = 0.03) of transfected cells into Env binding cells, respectively.
source: Cells engineered by the V434 or V781 strategies reproducibly converted an average of 1.75%(SD = 0.20) or 0.21%(SD = 0.03) of transfected cells into Env binding cells, respectively (Figure 2E).
evidence: The text explicitly states these engineering efficiencies and references Figure 2E showing the data.

claim: The universal editing strategy that removed 0.5 Mb of the IGHV locus was only about 8 times less efficient than the Ramos-specific strategy that replaces just 400 bp.
source: It was encouraging that the universal editing strategy that removed 0.5 Mb of the IGHV locus was only about 8 times less efficient than the Ramos-specific strategy that replaces just 400 bp.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the efficiency data presented (1.75% / 0.21% ≈ 8.3).

claim: A similar strategy was reported to remove up to 5 Mb of genomic DNA from chromosome 11 in mouse embryonic stem cells suggesting the method may work universally.
source: A similar strategy was reported to remove up to 5 Mb of genomic DNA from chromosome 11 in mouse embryonic stem cells suggesting the method may work universally (Kato et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kato et al., 2017.

claim: Sanger sequencing of PCR products confirmed that the new PG9 gene was grafted as expected between Cas9 cut sites within the IGHV locus by HDR.
source: Sanger sequencing of these products confirmed that the new PG9 gene was grafted as expected between Cas9 cut sites within the IGHV locus by HDR (Figure 2—figure supplements 3–5).
evidence: The text states this confirmation and references Figure 2—figure supplements 3–5 showing the sequence data.

claim: Amplification-free whole genome sequencing of C108 SOSIP-selected cells showed approximately 30x coverage depth for diploid regions of the genome.
source: Amplification-free whole genome sequencing of C108 SOSIP-selected cells (engineered with either the V434 or V781 strategy) was performed using fragmented gDNA from these lines using the Illumina HiSeq X. Reads were mapped to the human reference genome hg19 (International Human Genome Sequencing Consortium, 2004) showing approximately 30x coverage depth for diploid regions of the genome (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The text explicitly states the sequencing coverage and references Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: Coverage depth analysis was consistent with removal of the V781-J6 region in the expressed allele in C108 SOSIP-selected cells engineered with the universal strategy.
source: Coverage depth was consistent with removal of the V781-J6 region in the expressed allele in C108 SOSIP-selected cells engineered with the universal strategy, but not from the excluded allele which is not expressed due to a chromosomal translocation of the IGHV region to chr8 in this Burkitt's lymphoma line (Klein et al., 1975).
evidence: The text states this finding from the whole genome sequencing analysis.

claim: The excluded allele in Ramos cells is not expressed due to a chromosomal translocation of the IGHV region to chr8 in this Burkitt's lymphoma line.
source: Coverage depth was consistent with removal of the V781-J6 region in the expressed allele in C108 SOSIP-selected cells engineered with the universal strategy, but not from the excluded allele which is not expressed due to a chromosomal translocation of the IGHV region to chr8 in this Burkitt's lymphoma line (Klein et al., 1975).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Ramos cell line, supported by citation (Klein et al., 1975).

claim: Coverage depth analysis showed a deletion between the V3-11 and V3-7 genes in the excluded allele relative to the reference genome.
source: Coverage depth analysis showed a deletion between the V3-11 and V3-7 genes in the excluded allele (relative to the reference genome), and a D-J recombination event in this allele between D3-9 and the J6 gene that would have occurred during the maturation of this B cell in vivo.
evidence: The text states this finding from the whole genome sequencing analysis.

claim: A D-J recombination event occurred in the excluded allele between D3-9 and the J6 gene during the maturation of this B cell in vivo.
source: Coverage depth analysis showed a deletion between the V3-11 and V3-7 genes in the excluded allele (relative to the reference genome), and a D-J recombination event in this allele between D3-9 and the J6 gene that would have occurred during the maturation of this B cell in vivo.
evidence: The text states this finding from the whole genome sequencing analysis.

claim: The high read coverage depth for the 5' and 3' HRs in engineered cells suggests the integration of multiple donor DNAs by NHEJ mechanisms.
source: The high read coverage depth for the 5' and 3' HRs in engineered cells (especially using the V7-81 strategy), suggests the integration of multiple donor DNAs by NHEJ mechanisms (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is an inference based on the sequencing coverage data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: The presence of donor DNA backbone sequences on the outside of HR mapped reads confirms that integration did occur in both V781 and V434-engineered, C108 SOSIP-selected cells by NHEJ, in addition to the intended HR driven graft of PG9 VDJ into the expected sites.
source: The presence of donor DNA backbone sequences in this assembly on the outside of HR mapped reads (Figure 2—figure supplements 7–8) confirms that integration did occur in both V781 and V434-engineered, C108 SOSIP-selected cells by NHEJ, in addition to the intended HR driven graft of PG9 VDJ into the expected sites.
evidence: The text states this confirmation based on sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 7–8.

claim: It is normal for DNA introduced as plasmid to be incorporated into the mammalian genome at the site of dsDNA breaks non-specifically by NHEJ.
source: It is normal for DNA introduced as plasmid to be incorporated into the mammalian genome at the site of dsDNA breaks non-specifically by NHEJ (Vasquez et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about DNA repair mechanisms, supported by citation (Vasquez et al., 2001).

claim: The design should not allow for expression of PG9 HC when the donor is incorporated by most off-target repair mechanisms because the PG9 VDJ gene promoter must be in proximity to the downstream enhancer for transcription, and because the gene must be transcribed with the downstream constant gene and spliced in order to make a functional heavy chain protein.
source: Our design should not allow for expression of PG9 HC when the donor is incorporated by most off-target repair mechanisms because the PG9 VDJ gene promoter must be in proximity to the downstream enhancer for transcription, and because the gene must be transcribed with the downstream constant gene and spliced in order to make a functional heavy chain protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on the design of the donor DNA and requirements for functional HC expression.

claim: Some predicted, off-target editing events were detected by PCR in V781 PG9-engineered unselected or C108 SOSIP-selected cells.
source: Some predicted, off-target editing events were detected by PCR (Figure 2—figure supplement 9) in V781 PG9-engineered unselected or C108 SOSIP-selected cells.
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 2—figure supplement 9 showing the PCR data.

claim: Deletions between Cas9 cut sites were detected in unselected cells, but not in cells enriched for C108 SOSIP binding.
source: Deletions between Cas9 cut sites as have been previously reported to occur (Kato et al., 2017) were detected in unselected cells, but not in cells enriched for C108 SOSIP binding.
evidence: The text states this finding from the PCR analysis.

claim: One SOSIP selectable off-target donor DNA incorporation event was detected.
source: One SOSIP selectable off-target donor DNA incorporation event was detected. This event involved HDR within the 3' HR of the donor DNA, allowing for promoter activity (encoded within the 5'HR of the donor) and transcription with downstream constant regions for expression of functional PG9 HC, but with no accompanying 5' HDR from within the same donor DNA plasmid, indicated by the PCR product shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 9D.
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 2—figure supplement 9D showing the PCR data.

claim: Integration of donor DNA completely by NHEJ mechanisms was detected and appeared in both unselected and C108-selected cell lines.
source: Integration of donor DNA completely by NHEJ mechanisms was also detected and appeared in both unselected and C108-selected cell lines (Figure 2—figure supplement 9F).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 2—figure supplement 9F showing the PCR data.

claim: In vitro class switching occurs only in a specific Ramos sub-clone, 2G6.
source: It was previously shown that in vitro class switching occurs only in a specific Ramos sub-clone, 2G6 (Ford et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Ramos cell line, supported by citation (Ford et al., 1998).

claim: The engineered locus successfully transcribed PG9 and spliced it in the correct reading frame to either the native Ramos µ constant gene (PG9-IgM), or after culture with CD40 ligand-expressing feeder cells, IL-2 and IL-4, the native Ramos Y constant gene (PG9-IgG).
source: RT-PCR amplification using PG9 forward and IgM or IgG reverse primers generated amplicons which were sequenced to show that the engineered locus successfully transcribed PG9 and spliced it in the correct reading frame to either the native Ramos µ constant gene (PG9-IgM), or after culture with CD40 ligand-expressing feeder cells, IL-2 and IL-4, the native Ramos Y constant gene (PG9-IgG) (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 10).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 10 showing the sequence data.

claim: The engineered locus retained the ability to undergo isotype switching.
source: Thus, the engineered locus retained the ability to undergo isotype switching.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of PG9-IgG expression after cytokine stimulation.

claim: Random somatic hypermutation occurs in Ramos RA1 due to constitutive activity of AID.
source: While isotype switching is not inducible in Ramos RA1, random somatic hypermutation does occur due to constitutive activity of AID (Baughn et al., 2011; Sale and Neuberger, 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Ramos RA1 cell line, supported by citations (Baughn et al., 2011; Sale and Neuberger, 1998).

claim: Three rounds of selection and expansion in culture improved the binding of engineered cell lines to SOSIP probes in FACS experiments.
source: Three rounds of selection and expansion in culture improved the binding of engineered cell lines to SOSIP probes in FACS experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 3—figure supplement 1B showing the FACS data.

claim: A dominant change within the functional Ramos λLC was increasingly enriched in both MGRM8 and WITO SOSIP-selected lines at an AID hotspot, an S97N substitution within the CDRL3.
source: A dominant change within the functional Ramos λLC was increasingly enriched in both MGRM8 and WITO SOSIP-selected lines at an AID hotspot, an S97N substitution within the CDRL3.
evidence: The text states this finding from the NGS analysis of selected cell lines.

claim: The S97N mutation predicts a shift in a potential N-linked glycosylation site (PNGS) from N95 to 97.
source: This mutation predicts a shift in a potential N-linked glycosylation site (PNGS) from N95 to 97.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sequence change and knowledge of PNGS motifs.

claim: Coding changes resulting in the deletion of the PNGS glycan were also observed to a lesser degree.
source: Coding changes resulting in the deletion of this glycan were also observed to a lesser degree (Figure 3B).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 3B showing the sequence data.

claim: Antibodies with either S97G or S97N mutations generally improved affinity for HIV SOSIPs from different clades.
source: Antibodies with either of these mutations generally improved affinity for HIV SOSIPs from different clades (Figure 3C).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 3C showing the BLI data.

claim: The S97G and S97N mutations resulted in more potent neutralization of a number of HIV strains, including a virus from the panel designed to represent global HIV diversity, not neutralized by the original chimera.
source: Furthermore, these mutations resulted in more potent neutralization of a number of HIV strains, including a virus from the panel designed to represent global HIV diversity, not neutralized by the original chimera (Figure 3D).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 3D showing the neutralization data.

claim: The S97G and S97N mutants remained non-autoreactive in the HeP-2 assay.
source: These mutants remained non-autoreactive in the HeP-2 assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 4) and did not strongly alter expression based on SEC profiles (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 1—figure supplement 4 showing the HEp-2 assay data.

claim: The S97G and S97N mutants did not strongly alter expression based on SEC profiles.
source: These mutants remained non-autoreactive in the HeP-2 assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 4) and did not strongly alter expression based on SEC profiles (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 1—figure supplement 2 showing the SEC data.

claim: PG9 crystal structures and homology modeling suggest that, in the PG9-Ramos chimera, steric clashes involving the Ramos CDRL3 N-linked glycan at position 95 may impede access of the PG9 CDRH3 to its bnAb epitope.
source: PG9 crystal structures and homology modeling suggest that, in this chimera, steric clashes involving the Ramos CDRL3 N-linked glycan at position 95 may impede access of the PG9 CDRH3 to its bnAb epitope (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural modeling shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Breadth of neutralization by PG9 chimeras may be relatively easy to recover through affinity maturation by a number of possible pathways requiring few mutations to adapt the new light chain.
source: This result also suggests that breadth of neutralization by PG9 chimeras may be relatively easy to recover through affinity maturation by a number of possible pathways requiring few mutations to adapt the new light chain.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that few mutations improved neutralization.

claim: Clear differences from the starting PG9 VDJ gene sequences were observed in both PU and M3 data sets.
source: Clear differences from the starting PG9 VDJ gene sequences were observed in both data sets and the positions of many of these mutations appear to fall within regions known to be canonical AID hotspots (WRCY) (Smith et al., 1996) (Figure 3F).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 3F showing the mutation data.

claim: The positions of many mutations in the PG9 VDJ gene appear to fall within regions known to be canonical AID hotspots (WRCY).
source: Clear differences from the starting PG9 VDJ gene sequences were observed in both data sets and the positions of many of these mutations appear to fall within regions known to be canonical AID hotspots (WRCY) (Smith et al., 1996) (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is an observation based on comparison with known AID hotspot motifs, supported by citation (Smith et al., 1996).

claim: Genes being introduced into the locus undergo normal somatic hypermutation which could be manipulated through the use of codon optimization to encourage or discourage mutations at certain positions by modifying AID hotspot motifs in donor DNA-introduced antibody genes.
source: This suggests that genes being introduced into the locus undergo normal somatic hypermutation which could be manipulated through the use of codon optimization to encourage or discourage mutations at certain positions by modifying AID hotspot motifs in donor DNA-introduced antibody genes.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of mutations at AID hotspots.

claim: In engineered Ramos cells, PG9 expressed using the V3-74 promoter stained more brightly with the HIV envelope probe than did those using V7-81, presumably due to differing promoter strengths.
source: In engineered Ramos cells, PG9 expressed using the V3-74 promoter stained more brightly with the HIV envelope probe than did those using V7-81, presumably due to differing promoter strengths.
evidence: This is an observation with an inferred explanation about promoter strength.

claim: Engineering efficiency using V3-74 was routinely higher (0.35% of the live cell gate) compared with V7-81.
source: In addition, engineering efficiency was routinely higher (0.35% of the live cell gate) compared with V7-81 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 4—figure supplement 1 showing the data.

claim: Cell cycling and/or persistence in the S/G2 phases promote HDR.
source: Because cell cycling and/or persistence in the S/G2 phases promote HDR (Hung et al., 2018), we stained cells with CFSE to assess the dynamics of B cell division in order to correctly time the introduction of our engineering reagents.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation (Hung et al., 2018).
